realLife: DBSCAN suits map data and sensor hot spots, where clusters have odd shapes and some readings are simply stray.
summary: Compare k-means, DBSCAN and hierarchical clustering on shapes where they disagree.
headline: Different methods, different ideas of a cluster
overview: k-means thinks a cluster is a round blob around a centre. DBSCAN thinks it is a dense region separated from other dense regions, and leaves sparse points as noise. Hierarchical clustering repeatedly merges the two closest groups, and you choose where to cut.
None of them is correct in general. Which one fits depends on what shape you believe the groups have.

break.label: Break it
break.explains: Run k-means on two interleaved moons. A straight cut between two centres slices through both moons, so agreement with the true groups drops close to zero.

check.question: What does DBSCAN do with a point in a sparse region?
options: Forces it into the nearest cluster
Starts a new cluster for it

data: Moons, rings, blobs and blobs of unequal density. Agreement is the adjusted Rand index: 1 means the same grouping as the truth, about 0 means no better than chance.
maths: DBSCAN: a point is core if at least minPts points, itself included, lie within distance eps of it.
$$d_{\text{single}}=\min_{a\in A,\,b\in B}\lVert a-b\rVert,\qquad d_{\text{complete}}=\max_{a\in A,\,b\in B}\lVert a-b\rVert$$
Single linkage can chain through a thin bridge of points. Ward merges the pair that raises within-group variance least, so it behaves a bit like k-means.
code:
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN, AgglomerativeClustering
DBSCAN(eps=0.07, min_samples=4).fit_predict(X)
AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=3, linkage='ward').fit_predict(X)
